title: Gaṇeśa Goes Around the World
tease: Two brothers race around the world for a mango. One of them does not leave the room.

source.locus: Rudra Saṃhitā; also Skanda Purāṇa and the Tamil Vināyaka Purāṇam
source.traditionNote: Northern tellings make Kārttikeya the elder brother; Tamil tradition makes Gaṇeśa the elder, which is why Vināyaka is worshipped first. We tell the Tamil shape throughout. The differences are listed below rather than smoothed over.

blocks.text: «Nārada» left one mango in the house, and said that whoever ate it would know everything worth knowing. Then he left, quickly, the way people do when they have handed someone a problem.

There were two boys in that house, and each had a very different way of moving through the world. «Gaṇeśa», the elder, was round, rode a mouse, and was not fast at all. «Kārttikeya», the younger, was fast — and very proud of being fast. He had a peacock to ride and a spear in his hand.
Both of them wanted the mango.
_A race,_ said «Śiva». _Around the world. First one back gets it._ There was one prize and one condition: return after circling the world.

«Kārttikeya» was gone before the sentence finished, flying out on his peacock to do exactly what had been asked. «Gaṇeśa» looked at his mouse, and both of them could see that a race of speed was already lost.

So «Gaṇeśa» sat down and thought. He knew he could not win by making his mouse faster. He needed to understand what the race was really asking, and whether _around the world_ had only one possible meaning.
Then he got up, walked to his parents, and circled them slowly three times. He was not pretending to have travelled far; he was making an argument about what counted as his world.
And he said: _a world is the thing everything else is inside. Everything I have is inside the two of you. I have been round my world three times. Where is my mango?_
Śiva laughed. «Pārvatī» handed it over.

«Kārttikeya» came back days later, dusty and exhausted, having actually travelled around the world. «Gaṇeśa» was already eating the mango. «Kārttikeya» was furious, because he had obeyed the race exactly as it sounded. In the Tamil telling he went south to «Palani», where he stands with a staff as Daṇḍāyudhapāṇi.
One brother answered the race by travelling around the world. The other answered by asking what _world_ meant. Both moved; only one changed the question.
«Nārada» came to visit with one extraordinary mango for a house with two sons.
Whoever received the fruit, he said, would gain knowledge. There was only one mango.
He handed it to «Śiva» and «Pārvatī» and left them with the problem.
Their two sons were very different.
«Gaṇeśa», the elder in the Tamil telling, rode a mouse and knew speed was not his advantage.
«Kārttikeya» was fast, rode a peacock, carried a spear and was very used to winning races.
Both of them wanted the mango.
With one fruit and two sons, «Śiva» proposed a race around the world.
_A race,_ said Śiva. _Around the world. First one back gets it._
«Kārttikeya» left immediately on his peacock, taking the challenge exactly as it sounded.
He intended to circle the world properly and return first. Nothing about his effort was lazy or foolish.
«Gaṇeśa» looked at his mouse and knew a straight race was already lost.
So instead of chasing his brother, he stopped and thought.
So he sat down and thought about the exact words his father had used: _around the world._

«Gaṇeśa» did not have the answer immediately. Racing faster was impossible, so he asked a different question. What did _world_ mean to him, and what would it mean to circle the source of everything he had?
And then he got up, not because the mouse had become faster, but because the problem had become different.

He walked over to where his parents were sitting and circled them slowly. When he returned to his starting place, he had not travelled far. He was not claiming distance; he was saying that for him, his parents contained the world that mattered.
Then he did it again, and once more after that: three complete circumambulations around «Śiva» and «Pārvatī».
And he sat down in front of them and said: _a world is the thing everything else is inside. Everything I have is inside the two of you. I have been round my world three times. Where is my mango?_
Śiva laughed. Pārvatī gave him the mango.

«Pārvatī» did not give a long explanation. She handed him the mango because his answer had satisfied the challenge. The prize went to the son who had changed the meaning of the race without refusing to answer it.

When «Kārttikeya» finally returned, dusty and exhausted after actually travelling around the world, his elder brother was already eating the mango. The sight made the difference between their two answers impossible to ignore.
«Kārttikeya» was furious, and not without reason. He had done exactly what the race seemed to ask, spent himself doing it, and returned to find that a different interpretation had already won.
He argued about the rules. From his point of view, he had completed the harder journey and arrived to find the prize already gone. The story does not need us to pretend his anger was silly.

In the Tamil tradition, his anger carries him south to «Palani». There he stands as Daṇḍāyudhapāṇi, with a staff and simple cloth, having left the contest and its prize behind. The ending keeps the hurt as well as the cleverness.

Both boys answered the challenge. «Kārttikeya» travelled around the world. «Gaṇeśa» stopped to ask what _world_ meant before deciding how to move. One answer measured distance. The other measured relationship. That is why the story still leaves room to argue about which answer feels fair. The story keeps both the effort of the journey and the cleverness of the question in view.

linked.reason: another story where the small, unhurried person turns out to have understood the question

close.question: Gaṇeśa did not go round the world. Do you think he won fairly?
close.seed: Sometimes the clever answer is to check what the question actually meant.

ifTheyAsk.a: It is a fair thing to be annoyed about, and Kārttikeya certainly was. The honest answer is that Gaṇeśa did not break the rule — he read it differently, and his parents accepted the reading. Ask your child which they would have done. Most children under seven side with Gaṇeśa and most over ten side with his brother, which is interesting in itself.

Because he did the thing properly, at enormous cost, and lost to someone who did not leave the room. Younger brothers and sisters know that feeling precisely. The story does not punish him for it — it just tells you where he went, and that he is still there.

ifTheyAsk.q: Did he really have an elephant's head?
ifTheyAsk.a: Yes, in every telling — and how he got it is a separate story, and a harder one, involving his father not recognising him. That one is in the collection for older children. Tonight it is enough that he had it and that nobody in the room found it remarkable.
